This is the voice of Dominic James LaRocca, better known as Nick LaRocca, leader and manager of the world's first jazz band, known as the creators of jazz. I'll tell you about my early life in music and contact. I was born in 1889 in the city of New Orleans. My father's name was Geronimo LaRocca, who was a trumpet player like myself. My mother is Victoria D'Neena and out of that marriage came six children. I'll give you them in order. Rosario was the oldest. Antonia was my sister, was second. Maria was third. Bartholomew was four. I mean Dominic, Nick, that is me, was the fourth child. Bartholomew was the fifth child and Leonard was the sixth child. In my early life, the Italians or Germans and many people, they used to have birthday parties and different functions around the city. My father played in many bands about the city. And all he could get was free. He taught my sisters how to play. He taught my older brother how to play. And when it came to my turn, I was to become a doctor. He didn't want no music for me. But I craved music. And my early contact with music was out where my father would play like Spanish Ford or either the West End. And sometimes when he wasn't playing, he would take me out to White City and listen to the music. Or we'd go to the parks and listen to music. Or go on the river and listen to music. Because that was the main part of my father's trade. He was a shoe merchant. He sold shoes to the sailors and repaired them. And he spoke four different languages. My father lived, when he first opened his place at Washington Avenue in St. Thomas, he had a little shoe store and a shoe making place and repairing. And he made new shoes also. On a Sunday, when we weren't working, or my father wasn't working, he'd bring us out along the river, which was the Poor People's Promenade. At that time, they had no steamboats, steam ships. They had steamboats, but no steam ships. Ocean going that I seen. And the wharf was open to fail. And it was Poor People's Promenade. In the middle, they had boats that came from Portuguese. And each one of these boats had a band on them. Or sometimes a little accordion, or piccolo, or bass violin, or violin. The Italians were the same. They had a clarinet or piccolo with this accordion. It was a little bit octagon-shaped accordion that they played. And on Sundays, the Germans, I'm going ahead of my story. The Germans had all brass instruments. They had cornet, alto, baritone, and tuba. And they used a bass drum. And these men would go around the parts of the front part of the city, playing on the street corners, accepting gratuitous from the people with a hat. That was some of my musical education. And the more my father take me to these places, the more I was determined to play music. At the age of nine years old, I remember just as well as I am here today. I don't say that I have a better memory than anybody else. But we were going into Walwood, Spain. And they were just stringing the telephone wires and telegraph wires on St. Thomas Street, passing the street. They were putting up wires, telegraph wires. My uncle, Anthony Danina, had volunteered for the war to go to Spain. And all my mom, my dad and I was crying. So I stole this cornet and went down to the block and tried to learn this cornet. At first, I couldn't make no sounds out of it. I couldn't understand the way he would play it and play so easy with it. I was singing them out. I was blowing a note and another one. Then I got to playing bugle calls. Then we kids would go around the neighborhood way off from the house. And some would have wash bars, tin pans, and any old refuse kitchen utensil that they didn't use. Some had bricks, broomsticks, simulated soldiers. And they had an American flag, a little bit of piece of American flag that they had, because everybody had flags then. And they had a flag and they put it on a stick and it carried it. And down on Spain, we'd go all over the streets. We played a bugle call. That's all I knew. I later take in this cornet and I began to find all the notes what the keys was for. I took a piece of paper and the simple tunes that I knew like the chilling would sing. Here comes the boat around the bend. Goodbye my lover, goodbye. Loaded down with China men. came and appeared, Mrs. Alice, how do you pronounce her? Alice, Alice Kern. Alice Kern, K-I-E-R-N. A female person over the age of majority and full well known unto me notary public, who first being duly sworn, disposed and said as follows, that deponent was well acquainted with and has personally known for more than 25 years, one Dominic J. La Rocca, who resides in the city of New Orleans, state of Louisiana. A deponent is an organist by profession and during a period of time from 1914 to 1916, set down on paper various compositions originated by the said Dominic J. La Rocca, among which compositions was the number presently known as Tiger Ray, that the said Dominic J. La Rocca originated and played the aforementioned numbers by ear, not knowing the reading and writing of music, and would either play on his cornet or hum the mentioned numbers to deponent, that on the occasion when the said Dominic J. La Rocca first played Tiger Ray to deponent, it was the first time that deponent had ever heard same, and thereupon reduced same to writing, that deponent has always considered the aforementioned Dominic J. La Rocca as the composer and originator of the song, presently known as an entitled Tiger Ray. Signed, Mrs. Alice Kern. Sworn to and subscribed to before me this 12th day of June 1940, David L. Herman, Notre Republic.

Now, you wanted to ask me about the band that played in Bill Gallaty's band? This man could have been around my age, if he was living today, maybe a year too older than me. He may be the father of some of these Gallaty boys playing around today. That I don't know, because I have never met any of these boys. But they played in the downtown section. Bill Gallaty was the leader, or the manager of the band. And he played valve trombone. They had a boy by the name of Tots, I don't know his right name, played drums. Bull Wendler played the bass violin. And a fellow named by the name of Palaszczuk played clarinet, played clarinet, and I played the clarinet. I followed a boy in there by the name of a Dykeman or something like on that order, who played with him prior to me coming into his band. That is, I took odd jobs with him. I wasn't a regular member of any band. I played on the picture shows. Between 1912 and 14 or 13, I played on the picture shows. I played on the JS Excursion Boat. I was hired there as an extra man. And I played the St. Louis blues, then known to me as Jogo blues, without the middle strain in it. And I had played blues similar to that before I ever heard the St. Louis blues. In my early training at school, at the closing exercise, they had a number they called the Holy City. Well, I had learned this number. And during the, Mr. Sokola was the man who taught us how to go through our little parts in the play. And the whole group was singing. I was in the back singing, and I was making contra melody to this tune. And he called me out in front, and he says, I want you to sing this. Now, if these Negroes were so great, and they said they came to New York before me, or any other bands that came there, they never was noticed, and their music couldn't have been any different than if they were playing anywhere else in the world. But they noticed the Dixieland Jazz Band. We stood out, we made history. We played record. We're not only the pioneers, but this record, we left for posterity, a way of playing that has never been improved on to this day. The way we played was in fugue form. Any record that you pick out, I know nothing about music. I'm just a Negro scholar of music, but I went to too many operas, opera places where I could hear good music, and I seen how they played the background, the country melody, and different melodies against one another. I learned that at the French opera, when I worked down there handling lights, when I was just a male boy. I could see one person singing one tune, and another one singing against it, whether it was country melody or not. But that impressed me much in the late years that I was incorporated at. And what we had was nothing but a conversation of instruments. Well, take the liver stable blues, which I say to the clarinet, la-e-da-da, clarinet answer me, do-do-do-do-do-do. Look at me here. In 1918, the New Orleans papers, or the Times-Picayune, disowned us, and say that we were not from New Orleans. I'll ask Mr. Eickward to read this, Jazz and Jazzism, which is an editorial that appeared in the New Orleans Times-Picayune, June of 20, 1918. Mr. Eickward, would you please read that?

Jazz and Jazzism. Why is the jazz music, and therefore the jazz band? As well asked, why is the dime novel, or the grease-dripping doughnut? All are manifestations of a low streak in man's taste that has not yet come out in civilization's wash. Indeed, one might go farther, and say that jazz music is the indecent story, syncopated and counterpointed, like the improper anecdote. Also, in the view, it was listened to blushingly, behind closed doors and drawn curtains. But like all vices, it grew bolder until it dared, decent surrounded. And there was tolerated because of its oddity. We usually think of people as either musical or non-musical, as if there were a simple line separating two great classes. This fact is, however, that there are many mansions in the house of the muses. There is first the great assembly hall of the melody, where most of us take our seats at some time in our lives. But a lesser number pass on to inner sanctuaries of harmony, where the melodic sequence, the tune, as it most frequently is called, has infinitely less interest than the blending of notes and two chords. So the combining wavelengths will give new aesthetic sensations. This inner chord of harmony is where nearly all the truly great music is enjoyed. In the house there is, however, another apartment, properly speaking, down in the basement, a kind of servants' hall of rhythm. It is there we hear the hum of the Indian dance, the throb of the oriental tambourines and kettle drums, the clatter of the clogs, the click of slavic heels, the tumpety-tump of the Negro banjo, and in fact, the native dances of the world. Although commonly associated with melody, and less often with harmony also, rhythm is not necessarily music, and he who loves to keep time to the pulse of the orchestral performance by patting his foot upon the theatre floor, is not necessarily a music clapper. The ultramaritanists, in composition, go so far as to pronounce taboo upon rhythm, and even omit the perpendicular lines of their bars of written music, so that the risk of a monotonous pulsation is done away with. Prominently in the basement hall of rhythm is found ragtime, and of those most devoted to cult of the displaced ascent, there has developed a brotherhood of those who, devoid of harmonic and even of melodic instinct, love to fairly wallow in noise. On certain natures sound loud and meaningless has an exciting, almost an intoxicating effect, like crude colors and strong perfumes, the sight of flesh or the ascetic pleasure in blood. To such as these, the jazz music is a delight, and a dance to the unstable bray of the suck butt gives a sensational delight. More intense and quite different from the languor of the Viennese waltz or the refined sentiment and respectful emotion of an 18th century minuet. In the matter of the jazz, New Orleans is particularly interested, since it has been widely suggested that this particular form of musical vice had its birth in this city, that it came in fact from doubtful surroundings in our slums. We do not recognize the honor of parenthood, but to accept the atrocity in polite society and where it has crept in, we should make it a point of civic honor to suppress it. Its musical value is nil, and its possibilities of harm are great. That's all right.

Jazz and Jazzism, New Orleans, June 20, 1918. To the editor of the Times, Picayune. After carefully reading your interesting editorial, Jazz and Jazzism, it seems to me to display profound shallowness. I am no defender of jazz, but I think you should recognize it for what it is, the style of playing. Compare it to the dime novel, if you will, but not to the grease-dripping donut, which is as aesthetic as a tidbit as any highbrow chef could concoct. Jazz may better be compared to the daring style in skirts, which are departures from what was proper a few years ago, and sometimes displays, sometimes display things not beautiful. Jazz, a departure from the proper in music, may display things not beautiful. It revels in close harmony and noise. As many classic compositions are full of close harmony and noise also, these things should not condemn jazz. Now, a hint that rhythm can also be dispensed with, the blending of notes into chords, so that combining wavelengths give new aesthetic sensations, being sufficient to produce a beautiful musical structure. As easily dabbed colors carelessly on canvas and produce beautiful pictures. Without structure and pulsation, there is no life. Human throbbing is necessary, even in the classical. Otherwise, there is no appeal to emotion, and without emotion it becomes nothing. Classical music carries constant appeal to the emotions by means of the throbbing and noise you ascribe to jazz. Jazz music may call to the sensual in some people, but I prefer to consider it merely the same appeal that makes men want to march or dance. Like wine, it quickens the pulse. No one will say the effect in the...is the same in everyone. Even so, it is an effect the masters of music have striven for, though you whitewash it by calling it refined sentiment and languor of a Vietnamese waltz. Fair play.
Mm-hmm. Fair play.

segments.title: Birth, family and first hearing music in New Orleans
segments.summary: La Rocca names his parents and siblings, his shoemaker father who played trumpet, riverfront and park music, and how at nine he took a cornet and taught himself tunes.

segments.title: Old New Orleans, Miss Young and Henry Young, first bands on the Gulf Coast
segments.summary: He recalls the city before cars, practising in the shoe store, his father's death, learning to fake with the Youngs, and forming his first groups in Long Beach and New Orleans.

segments.title: Free groups, 'no beer no music' bands, and his own band of 1918
segments.summary: He lists the downtown and uptown groups he played with for free, then taking outside jobs, picture shows, and having his tunes written down.

segments.title: Alice Kern affidavit on Tiger Rag authorship
segments.summary: The reader reads a 1940 sworn affidavit by organist Alice Kern that she wrote down La Rocca's compositions including Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Gallaty's band, odd jobs, the blues and 'not from Africa'
segments.summary: He describes Bill Gallaty's band members, his picture-show and excursion boat work, and argues that blues and his tunes derive from white sources, not Africa.

segments.title: Fidgety Feet, Tiger Rag themes and the Dixieland Jazz Band's New York debut
segments.summary: He explains where his tunes' ideas came from and recounts opening in New York in 1917, claiming priority over the Creole band and criticizing Stearns and Souchon.

segments.title: Variety 1917 article on jazz bands in cabarets
segments.summary: The reader reads a 1917 Variety item on jazz bands drawing crowds at New York cabarets.

segments.title: Why the Dixieland band stood out: playing in fugue form
segments.summary: He argues the band made history because its records interweaved three distinct melodies like a conversation of instruments, an idea from opera.

segments.title: Times-Picayune editorial 'Jazz and Jazzism' (1918)
segments.summary: La Rocca says New Orleans papers disowned the band, and the reader reads a hostile 1918 editorial condemning jazz.

segments.title: Reader's reply letter defending jazz
segments.summary: La Rocca introduces and the reader reads a letter to the editor answering the editorial.

segments.title: Second letter 'Ragtime jazz and operatic music', signed MC
segments.summary: La Rocca says jazz did not exist in New Orleans then; the reader reads a letter signed MC, followed by banter.

segments.title: How he made his tunes from opera; segregation and Lizzie Miles on the boat
segments.summary: He says his tunes came from chord construction and opera, then rails against mixed bands, a jazz club boat program and Stearns's letter, defending his views on segregation.

segments.title: More 1918 Times-Picayune letters on ragtime and jazz
segments.summary: The reader reads further letters to the editor defending ragtime and jazz.

segments.chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
segments.title: Victor circular for the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, March 1917
segments.summary: La Rocca has a Victor circular read praising the band's Livery Stable Blues record.

segments.chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
segments.title: Playing King Oliver's Canal Street Blues against the Dixieland records
segments.summary: He plays Oliver's record and claims its stop and clarinet part come from his band's earlier records, then plays his own cornet part.

segments.chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
segments.title: Claim that Black bands heard the Dixieland records and copied them
segments.summary: He argues the banjo and rhythm on the Oliver record were taken from the Dixieland recordings and makes demeaning remarks about Black musicians.

segments.chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's Sweet Little Papa compared with Ostrich Walk and All Night Long
segments.summary: He plays Armstrong's record and others to show the same stop time and chord construction came from his band's earlier records.

segments.chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
segments.title: Tiger Rag recording conditions, Kid Ory comparison and W.C. Handy's record
segments.summary: He compares a recent Ory record with the 1918 Tiger Rag, describes acoustic recording setup, and plays a Handy Columbia record while disputing Handy's claims.

segments.title: Handy's band and the Louisiana Five, Alcide Nunez
segments.summary: He says Handy's band was brought to New York to compete and failed, then discusses the Louisiana Five and his acquaintance with its clarinetist.

segments.title: Other bands that came to New York and failed; his notes as proof
segments.summary: He lists later New Orleans groups that failed in New York, argues with the interviewer over sources, and says he kept notes as proof.
